metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.limits: No cross-language byte/line-count comparison table was produced in this shard (assigned languages = Kotlin only); comparison is against idiomatic-best-practice expectation for the same frozen algorithm as required by language_quality.md fairness rules, not against a fabricated multi-language corpus.
metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.method: Qualitative + structural analysis of sampled Kotlin micro-benchmark and adversarial programs under template/programs/kotlin/{micro,adversarial}. Assessed token/line density needed to express the same algorithmic workload relative to idiomatic Kotlin best practices (no artificial verbosity or golfing).
observations: Kotlin's type inference (val/var without explicit types), default/named arguments, single-expression functions, and data classes (e.g. Mb04Result) let the mb04.kt workload express a 4-accumulator double-precision benchmark with minimal boilerplate compared to languages requiring explicit getters/setters or verbose type annotations.
String templates and String.format with Locale.ROOT keep output formatting compact and unambiguous in one line, versus multi-line formatting boilerplate needed in some other JVM-family languages.
Range expressions (0 until M) and modulo indexing avoid manual loop-counter boilerplate.

No need for explicit checked-exception handling or verbose collection boilerplate (e.g. no explicit ArrayList<Double> generic ceremony where DoubleArray primitives suffice), avoiding boxing overhead while staying concise.

Adversarial programs (ADV-01..26) are intentionally short/minimal snippets (170-600 bytes) demonstrating that Kotlin syntax does not force incidental verbosity even for edge-case language-feature probes.
metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.score_rationale: Kotlin ranks near the top of the assigned set for conciseness: strong type inference, expression-oriented syntax, data classes, extension-friendly stdlib, and lack of mandatory ceremony (no semicolons required, no mandatory access modifiers, smart casts) reduce code volume for equivalent semantics without sacrificing clarity. Score of 88/100 reflects this being very strong but not maximal versus more terse scripting-style languages for these particular numeric/loop-heavy micro-benchmarks, where explicit types are still written in some benchmark code for documentation/interop clarity (e.g. class Lcg(private var state: Long)).

metric.readability.limits: Assessment covers the sampled micro and adversarial Kotlin sources readable under this shard's permissions; full corpus (all ADV-*/mb* files) was listed but not every file's contents were individually read given turn budget.
metric.readability.method: Qualitative review of naming, structure, comments, and control flow in the same sampled Kotlin files, judged against idiomatic Kotlin style conventions (official Kotlin coding conventions).
observations: Consistent naming conventions (camelCase for functions/vars, PascalCase for classes) matching Kotlin's official style guide are used throughout mb04.kt and companion files.

Comments annotate spec-derived invariants (e.g. anti-elimination note, Locale.ROOT rationale, ITER flush timing) directly at point of relevance, aiding comprehension of non-obvious frozen-benchmark requirements.
Null-safety operators (?:, ?.) used idiomatically for defaulting (args[1].toIntOrNull() ?: 7), making intent explicit without try/catch noise.
Single-purpose small classes (Lcg, Mb04Result) with minimal public surface improve local readability; no deep nesting or long parameter lists observed in sampled files.
Explicit visibility modifiers (private var state) and immutability preference (val over var where possible) communicate intent clearly.
Adversarial-suite files are deliberately minimal single-purpose snippets, each isolating one language-feature probe, which is inherently easy to read in isolation.
metric.readability.score_rationale: Kotlin scores very high (90/100) for readability: null-safety syntax, smart casts, string templates, and expression-based control flow reduce boilerplate noise while explicit typing where used aids clarity for numeric-heavy code. Minor deduction versus a perfect score reflects occasional density from combined functional/OOP idioms (e.g. chained scope functions) that can require Kotlin-specific familiarity, though none of that was observed as overused in the sampled benchmark files.
